passages.text: Many writers and composers have insisted that their best ideas arrived not at the desk but during long walks. For decades such testimony was dismissed as romantic anecdote, until two psychologists at Stanford University subjected it to an experimental test in 2014. Participants were asked to devise as many novel uses as they could for ordinary objects, such as a tire or a button, either while seated or while walking on a treadmill facing a blank wall. Judges then rated every answer. The walkers produced responses which were rated considerably higher in ____, the very quality that artists had long attributed to their strolls, and the advantage persisted briefly after they sat down again. Notably, the setting hardly mattered; even a monotonous indoor treadmill was sufficient. What seems to count is the motion of the body itself, which apparently loosens the habitual grip of concentrated thought.

____ A popular belief holds that a camel stores water in its hump and draws on it during long journeys across the desert. In fact, the hump is largely a reservoir of fat, which the animal can metabolize for energy when food is scarce. Concentrating fat in one place also helps the camel stay cool, since insulation spread evenly over its body would trap heat. The camel's real defense against thirst lies elsewhere. Its kidneys produce highly concentrated urine, its oval red blood cells keep circulating even when the blood thickens, and its body temperature is permitted to climb several degrees during the day before any water is expended on sweating. When it finally reaches a well, a parched camel can swallow an astonishing volume in a matter of minutes.

The humble food can traces its origins to the Napoleonic era. Around the turn of the nineteenth century, a Parisian confectioner named Nicolas Appert began experimenting with ways to keep food from spoiling. He eventually settled on a method: he sealed food in glass bottles stopped with cork and then heated the bottles in boiling water for long periods. In 1810 the French government awarded him twelve thousand francs on condition that he publish his technique, since preserved rations promised to feed armies far from home. Appert had no idea why his bottles kept their contents fresh; the microbes which cause decay would not be understood until the work of Louis Pasteur half a century later. ____, the method proved reliable enough to spread to factories across Europe and America, where tin cans soon replaced fragile glass, and the industry it founded has long outlived the wars which inspired it.

In October 2024, tens of thousands of dockworkers walked off the job at ports along the East and Gulf Coasts of the United States, halting much of the country's container traffic for three days. Wages were part of the dispute, but the issue which proved hardest to resolve was automation. Many of the world's busiest terminals, from Rotterdam to Shanghai, now rely on remotely operated cranes and driverless vehicles which shuttle containers across the yard with minimal human intervention. Port operators contend that such machinery improves safety, eases congestion, and lets terminals operate around the clock. The union countered that automated equipment eliminates well-paid jobs and has not consistently delivered the promised efficiency. The contract finally agreed upon the following January combined substantial raises with provisions restricting fully automated equipment. The episode illustrates a broader dilemma: technologies which promise an industry higher productivity can appear, to those employed in it, primarily as a threat to their livelihood.

To a honeybee, a meadow looks very different from the way it looks to us. [A] Bees perceive ultraviolet light, and many petals bear markings drawn in it, patterns invisible to people because the wavelengths are too short for human eyes to detect. [B] Such photographs often show petals which reflect ultraviolet light at their tips but absorb it near the center, creating a dark bull's-eye that directs the insect toward the nectar. [C] Botanists call these markings nectar guides, and experiments suggest that bees locate food more quickly on flowers which display them. [D] The arrangement benefits both parties, since a bee which lands accurately wastes less energy and the plant has its pollen carried more reliably. [E] Some flowers even change color once they have been pollinated, steering visitors toward blossoms which still need their services.

In 1843 Ada Lovelace, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, published an English translation of an article by the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea describing Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine. [A] The machine was never completed, but its design anticipated many features of a modern computer, including a memory and a separate unit for performing calculations. [B] Lovelace's annotations on the article ended up nearly three times as long as the original. [C] In one of them she set out a step-by-step method for calculating a sequence known as the Bernoulli numbers, which is often described as the first published computer program. [D] More striking still was her speculation that such an engine might manipulate symbols of any kind, composing elaborate pieces of music, for instance, if the relations between notes could be expressed in its notation. [E] Where Babbage envisioned a powerful calculator, Lovelace glimpsed a general-purpose machine.

Across nearly every professional sport, teams win more often in their own stadiums than on the road. [A] The pattern, known as home advantage, has been documented in leagues ranging from football and basketball to ice hockey. [B] Visiting teams consistently score fewer goals and concede more, even against opponents of similar strength. [C] Part of the gap is a matter of travel: visitors arrive weary from long journeys and must perform in unfamiliar surroundings. [D] Seasons played in empty stadiums, which many leagues were forced to stage in 2020, allowed researchers to disentangle these two causes, since the travel remained while the spectators vanished. [E] In many of those leagues the home advantage shrank noticeably, and referees' bias against visiting players shrank sharply, suggesting that the roar of the stands had indeed been swaying the officials.

Rates of asthma and allergies have climbed steeply in wealthy countries over recent decades, and in several of them close to one child in ten has now been diagnosed with asthma. [A] The pressurized inhaler, introduced in the 1950s, was among the first devices to deliver a measured dose of medicine directly to the lungs. [B] Because the increase has unfolded far too rapidly to be explained by changes in genes, researchers have sought its causes in the way children now live. [C] One revealing comparison involved two farming communities in the United States, the Amish of Indiana and the Hutterites of South Dakota, which share similar ancestry and habits. [D] Yet asthma proved roughly four times as common among Hutterite children, whose families farm with modern machinery, as among Amish children, who grow up beside barns full of animals. [E] Dust from Amish homes, which was far richer in microbial material, appeared to train the children's immune systems to react less violently. Mice exposed to the same dust were likewise protected against inflamed airways.

In 1930 the British linguist Charles Kay Ogden published a book introducing Basic English, a simplified version of the language which he hoped would serve the world as an international auxiliary tongue. [A] Ogden believed that a shared language, simple enough for almost anyone to master in a few weeks, could ease commerce and reduce misunderstanding between nations. [B] He designed the system to be learned quickly: its entire vocabulary consists of just 850 words, and a mere eighteen 'operators' (basic verbs), such as get, put, and make, express actions which ordinary English conveys with hundreds of different verbs. [C] Some critics objected that the resulting sentences were clumsy and that a learner would still be unable to follow ordinary English. [D] Basic English never became the global second language its creator envisioned, yet its spirit survives in news programs and encyclopedias written in deliberately simplified English. [E] Cambridge, where Ogden studied, is among the oldest universities in the English-speaking world, having been founded early in the thirteenth century. Their writers still limit themselves to a short list of common words so that learners can follow along.

Few words are used as widely as OK, which turns up in dozens of languages around the world. Its origin, however, was long a subject of colorful speculation.
(A) Most of those coinages vanished quickly. OK survived, partly because it was soon adopted as a slogan in the presidential election of 1840, when supporters of Martin Van Buren, whose nickname was Old Kinderhook, organized OK Clubs.
(B) The puzzle was largely solved in the 1960s by the American scholar Allen Walker Read, who traced the term to a Boston newspaper in 1839. At that time, young writers in the city enjoyed a fashion for comic abbreviations of deliberately misspelled phrases, such as O.W. for oll wright.
(C) Among them was oll korrect, a playful spelling of all correct, which was shortened to O.K. Had the joke remained a passing fad, the word would probably have been forgotten along with its companions.

The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics went to two scientists whose work had long seemed to belong more to computer science than to physics. John Hopfield, an American physicist, devised in 1982 a network of interconnected nodes which could store patterns and reconstruct a complete pattern from a partial or distorted version, much as a person can recognize a familiar face in a blurred photograph. Geoffrey Hinton, a British-Canadian computer scientist, built on that idea with a model that drew on the statistical physics of systems composed of many interacting parts. The Nobel committee emphasized that both researchers had borrowed concepts from physics to create the artificial neural networks underlying today's machine learning. The award was not without irony. Hinton, who left his position at Google in 2023, has since become one of the most prominent voices warning that the technology he helped create could pose grave risks if it is not carefully controlled.

Before the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was a slow, labor-intensive affair. Dockworkers carried sacks, barrels, and crates aboard one by one, and a vessel might spend nearly as long in port being loaded and unloaded as it did at sea. In 1956 the American trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean sent a converted tanker, the Ideal X, from New Jersey to Texas carrying fifty-eight metal boxes which could be lifted directly from truck trailers onto the ship. The concept of standardized containers spread rapidly once international agreements fixed their dimensions, allowing the same box to move seamlessly among ships, trains, and trucks without its contents ever being touched. The consequences were profound. Shipping costs fell so dramatically that it became economical to manufacture goods on one continent and sell them on another. Meanwhile, old waterfront districts emptied out, as container terminals demanded vast open yards and far fewer laborers than the crowded piers they replaced.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome aboard. Before we begin, please make sure your audio guide is switched on; the volume control is on the side. We're standing on the deck of a cargo steamer which carried rice and timber along this coast for nearly forty years before being retired and restored. In a moment we'll go below to the engine room, which is narrow and steep, so please keep at least one hand on the rail. Down there you'll see the original boiler. The crew called <u>it</u> the Old Lady, and a careless stoker who let its water run low could make it explode, so they treated it with a mixture of affection and dread. After the engine room, we'll visit the crew's quarters, where eight men slept in a space smaller than most modern kitchens. The tour lasts about forty minutes, and photographs are welcome everywhere except the captain's cabin, where fragile charts are kept away from bright light.

In a famous study published in 1968, the psychologist Robert Rosenthal and the school principal Lenore Jacobson gave pupils at a California elementary school an intelligence test and then told teachers that certain children were about to experience a spurt of intellectual growth. In reality, those children had been chosen at random. When the pupils were tested again months later, the selected children, particularly in the youngest grades, had gained more than their classmates. The researchers argued that teachers' expectations had subtly shaped their conduct: they may have offered the chosen pupils warmer encouragement, more challenging questions, and more time to respond. Subsequent studies have shown that such expectancy effects are real but usually modest, and some critics have questioned the original analysis. Still, the broader lesson has endured. What a teacher believes about a student's potential can, through countless small interactions, become part of the reason that potential is or is not realized.

In 2010 two Harvard psychologists, Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert, used a smartphone app to contact thousands of adults at random moments during the day. Each time, participants reported what they were doing, whether they were thinking about something other than that activity, and how happy they felt. The results were striking. People's minds were wandering nearly half the time, and the proportion was substantial during almost every activity measured. The link to mood was equally notable: people were less happy when their minds wandered than when they were focused, and even pleasant daydreams left them no happier than attention to the task at hand.
The researchers concluded that a wandering mind is an unhappy mind, but the relationship may be more ____ than that slogan implies. Other studies suggest that mind wandering helps people plan for the future, rehearse conversations, and stumble upon creative solutions to problems they had set aside. Daydreaming may become harmful mainly when it turns into rumination, the repetitive dwelling on worries and regrets. The capacity to let attention drift, in other words, is not simply a flaw to be eradicated. It is a mental tool whose effects depend largely on where, and how often, the mind chooses to go.

Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a seaside town on the southern coast of England whose crumbling cliffs regularly exposed the remains of ancient marine creatures. [A] Her family was poor, and selling curiosities to tourists helped them survive after her father died when she was eleven. [B] Around that time, Mary and her brother uncovered the skeleton of an ichthyosaur, a reptile which resembled a dolphin. [C] Over the following decades she found the first complete plesiosaur skeleton and one of the first pterosaurs discovered outside Germany, and she became adept at reading the cliffs after storms, when fresh fossils were most likely to appear. [D] Yet as a woman, and a working-class one, she could not join the Geological Society of London, and the gentlemen who purchased her specimens frequently described them in print without acknowledging her. [E] Only after her death in 1847 did her contribution receive wider recognition, and today historians regard her as one of the most influential fossil hunters of her era.

On January 5, 2025, New York City began charging most drivers a toll to enter the busiest part of Manhattan, becoming the first American city to adopt congestion pricing. The idea is hardly new. London introduced a similar charge in 2003, and Stockholm made one permanent in 2007 after a trial period and a referendum. Economists have long favored such schemes because road space in a crowded city center is a scarce resource which drivers otherwise consume without paying for the delays they impose on everyone else. ____, a toll can make each driver weigh the true cost of a trip, while the revenue can be invested in public transit.
Congestion charges are rarely popular at first. In Stockholm, opinion polls showed most residents opposed to the charge before the trial began, yet support grew once people experienced shorter journeys and quieter streets. New York's program faced lawsuits and fierce political opposition, and early reports of reduced traffic were greeted with both celebration and skepticism. Whether the plan endures may depend less on economic theory than on whether commuters come to believe, as many Stockholm residents eventually did, that the benefits justify the price.

In 1982 the social scientists James Q. Wilson and George Kelling published an influential magazine article arguing that visible signs of disorder in a neighborhood, such as broken windows, graffiti, and litter, signal that no one is in charge. In their view, leaving such minor problems unrepaired invites more serious offenses, because potential wrongdoers conclude that they are unlikely to be challenged. The theory inspired police departments in New York and elsewhere to crack down on petty violations like fare evasion. Crime in the city fell dramatically during the 1990s, but the decline cannot be attributed to the policy with any certainty, since crime dropped sharply in many cities which adopted no such strategy. Critics also note that aggressive enforcement against minor offenses fell most heavily on poor and minority residents. The theory's legacy, then, remains ____: admired by some as common sense and condemned by others as a pretext for heavy-handed policing. Few ideas in criminology have provoked such sharply divided reactions.

Each satellite in the Global Positioning System carries an atomic clock, and a receiver on the ground calculates its location by comparing time signals from several satellites. Because radio signals travel at the speed of light, an error of a single microsecond would shift a calculated position by about three hundred meters. Einstein's theories of relativity therefore become a practical engineering concern. (A) ____, the satellites move fast relative to the ground, and according to special relativity their clocks should tick slightly slower than ours. (B) ____, they orbit far from Earth's center, where gravity is weaker, and general relativity predicts that clocks there should run faster. The second effect is larger, so the satellite clocks gain roughly thirty-eight microseconds a day. Engineers adjust the clocks' frequency before launch to compensate; without that correction, navigation errors would accumulate by several kilometers each day.

____ In a well-known experiment, a team of American psychologists paid volunteers five dollars for completing a survey and then invited them to donate some of it to a children's charity. Some volunteers read statistics describing millions of people facing hunger across several African countries. Others saw a photograph of a single seven-year-old girl from Mali named Rokia and read a brief description of her poverty. Those who met Rokia gave roughly twice as much as those who read the statistics. Strikingly, when a third group received both the photograph and the numbers, donations fell back toward the lower level, as if the figures dulled the feelings which the girl had aroused. Comparable effects appear well beyond the laboratory, as when a single trapped child draws more attention and money than a famine affecting entire regions.

The American journalist Nellie Bly set out from New York in 1889 to test whether a person could circle the globe faster than the fictional hero of Jules Verne's novel Around the World in Eighty Days. Traveling by steamship and train, and carrying little more than a single small bag, she crossed the Atlantic, passed through Europe, the Suez Canal, and Asia, and returned across the Pacific and the American continent. Her newspaper turned the journey into a sensation, publishing regular dispatches and inviting readers to guess the exact time of her return. She arrived back in New York seventy-two days after her departure, setting a world record. The stunt suited her reputation. Bly was already celebrated for an audacious ____ two years earlier, in which she had feigned insanity to get herself committed to an asylum for women and then exposed the brutal conditions she found inside. That report had prompted a grand jury investigation and a substantial increase in public funding for the city's asylums.

Few images are as instantly recognizable as The Great Wave off Kanagawa, the woodblock print in which a towering wave curls over three fishing boats while Mount Fuji sits small and serene in the distance. Katsushika Hokusai produced it around 1831, when he was already in his seventies, as part of a series called Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. Much of the print's striking effect comes from its color. Hokusai made lavish use of Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment that a color maker in Berlin had discovered accidentally early in the eighteenth century and that had only recently become affordable in Japan. Unlike the plant-based blues on which Japanese printmakers had relied, which faded quickly, the imported pigment was intense and durable. Its arrival coincided with a vogue for landscape prints, and publishers marketed the series partly on the novelty of its color. A pigment invented by accident in Europe thus helped shape one of the most celebrated works of Japanese art.

The Panama Canal depends on fresh water in a way that many people do not realize. [A] Ships passing between the Atlantic and the Pacific are raised and lowered by a series of locks, and each transit releases millions of liters of water from Gatun Lake, an artificial reservoir fed by rainfall, into the sea. [B] In 2023 an unusually severe drought, linked in part to the El Nino climate pattern, left the lake's level perilously low. [C] The canal authority responded by reducing the number of daily transits and limiting how deeply loaded ships could be. [D] Faced with such delays, some shippers paid enormous sums at auction for scarce passage slots, while others opted for longer routes around South America or through the Suez Canal. [E] Rainfall returned the following year and restrictions were gradually eased, but the episode prompted plans to secure additional water, including a proposed reservoir on a nearby river.

Every day, cargo ships carry enormous quantities of seawater across the oceans. [A] To stay stable when their holds are empty, ships pump water into ballast tanks at one port and discharge it at another, and with that water travel countless larvae, plankton, and small fish. [B] Since a large vessel may release vast volumes at once, even a few survivors can found a population in a new harbor. [C] In the late 1980s zebra mussels, native to the Black and Caspian Sea region, were discovered in the Great Lakes of North America, most likely delivered in ballast tanks. [D] The mussels multiplied explosively, clogging the intake pipes of power plants and water utilities. [E] Under an international convention which entered into force in 2017, ships must now treat or exchange their ballast water before releasing it.

Australia is one of a small number of democracies in which voting is compulsory. [A] Since 1924, citizens enrolled for federal elections have been legally obliged to cast a ballot, and those who fail to do so without a valid reason receive a modest fine. [B] Turnout in Australian federal elections has usually exceeded ninety percent, far above the levels typical of countries where voting is voluntary. [C] Moreover, Australia's capital, Canberra, was purpose-built after a design competition won by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin. [D] Supporters argue that compulsion produces a parliament reflecting the entire population rather than only its most motivated or affluent citizens. [E] Critics reply that forcing people to vote infringes on individual liberty and may fill ballot boxes with uninformed choices, although the obligation in practice amounts to attending a polling place, since the ballot itself is secret and may be left blank.

Pacific salmon hatch in freshwater streams, migrate to the ocean, and spend several years feeding in the open sea before returning to spawn. [A] Remarkably, most of them return not merely to the right river but to the very stream in which they hatched, sometimes after journeys of more than a thousand kilometers. [B] In the open ocean they appear to navigate by sensing Earth's magnetic field, which guides them to the general region of their home coast. [C] Once they reach fresh water, smell takes over: young salmon memorize the distinctive chemical signature of their native stream, and adults follow that scent upstream, choosing the correct branch at every fork. [D] Experiments in which researchers plugged the nostrils of returning fish showed that they were then far more likely to stray into the wrong stream, confirming how heavily the final stage of the journey relies on scent. [E] In addition, wild salmon is prized by chefs for its rich flavor and is often considered more nutritious than farmed fish. Few migrations in the animal kingdom demand such precision, and fewer still end, as the salmon's does, in the very place where life began.

In the late 1960s, the psychologists Martin Seligman and Steven Maier conducted a series of animal experiments that would shape decades of research on depression.
(A) Dogs from the first group quickly learned to leap over the barrier, just as untrained animals did. Their earlier experience of control seemed to carry over into the new situation.
(B) The second group behaved very differently. Most of those dogs lay down and endured the shocks, even though relief was only a short jump away. Having learned that their actions made no difference, they had apparently stopped trying. Seligman called this state learned helplessness and proposed it as a model of human depression.
(C) Dogs were first exposed to mild electric shocks. Some could terminate the shocks by pressing a panel with their noses, while others, receiving identical shocks, had no means of control. Later, all the dogs were placed in a box where they could escape the shocks simply by leaping over a low barrier.

In the early twentieth century, pellagra, a disease marked by skin rashes, diarrhea, and mental confusion, killed thousands of people each year in the American South. Most physicians believed it was an infection, but Joseph Goldberger, a doctor with the US Public Health Service, noticed a revealing pattern: in orphanages and asylums the disease was <u>common</u> among the inmates yet almost unknown among the staff who lived alongside them. A germ, he reasoned, would not discriminate in this way, and he suspected the monotonous diet of corn bread, molasses, and fat pork served to the inmates. When he added milk, meat, and vegetables to the meals at two orphanages, pellagra <u>multiplied</u> among the children. Yet many of his colleagues <u>resisted</u> his conclusion, and some Southern leaders found the suggestion that poverty was making people sick <u>offensive</u>. Only after the vitamin niacin was identified as the missing nutrient in 1937 did his view gain general <u>acceptance</u>.

Shipping carries most of the world's traded goods and accounts for a significant share of global greenhouse gas emissions, most of it from burning heavy fuel oil. In 2023 the International Maritime Organization, the United Nations agency which regulates shipping, adopted a strategy aiming for net-zero emissions from the industry by or around 2050. Meeting that goal will require new fuels, and ammonia has emerged as one of the leading candidates. Because its molecule contains no carbon, ammonia releases no carbon dioxide when burned, and it can be stored as a liquid under moderate pressure or modest cooling, unlike hydrogen, which must be chilled to extremely low temperatures. The fuel has serious drawbacks, however. Ammonia is highly toxic, so a leak at sea could endanger crews and marine life, and burning it can release nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas, unless engines are meticulously designed. Moreover, most ammonia today is produced from natural gas, so its climate benefits hinge on cleaner methods of manufacture.

At four in the morning the airport looks deserted from the outside, but from up here it never really sleeps. The overnight cargo flights arrive in clusters, and each one needs a runway, a taxi route, and a parking position assigned before its wheels touch the ground. My screen shows every aircraft within forty miles as a small tag of letters and numbers, and my headset carries a steady stream of pilots reading back the instructions I give them. Most of the job is routine, but routine is exactly what we labor to preserve. If fog rolls in off the bay, I may have to widen the spacing between arrivals and hold some planes in a slow circle above the city. The hardest part is not any single decision but staying alert through the empty hours, when the radio falls silent for long stretches and it would be easy to let my attention drift. When my relief arrives at six, I hand over my picture of the sky as conscientiously as a nurse hands over a patient.

In 1900 the British archaeologist Arthur Evans began excavating the palace at Knossos on Crete and uncovered thousands of clay tablets inscribed in an unknown script. He called it Linear B, and for half a century it resisted every attempt at decipherment. Most scholars, Evans included, assumed it recorded a lost language of the Minoan civilization. The breakthrough came from Michael Ventris, an English architect who had been fascinated by the script since hearing Evans lecture when he was a schoolboy. Building on meticulous work by the American classicist Alice Kober, who had identified patterns of word endings suggesting an inflected language, Ventris constructed grids relating the symbols to probable sounds. In 1952, to his own astonishment, the words which emerged were recognizably an early form of Greek. The discovery pushed back the written record of the Greek language by several centuries and revealed that the tablets were largely mundane administrative records: inventories of livestock, chariots, and jars of oil.

In 1968 Spencer Silver, a chemist at the American company 3M, was trying to develop an exceptionally strong adhesive for use in aircraft construction. Instead, he produced the opposite: a glue which clung lightly to surfaces and could be peeled away without leaving a residue. The substance was intriguing, but no one at the company could think of a practical use for it, and for years Silver promoted it to colleagues with little success.
The solution came from Art Fry, another 3M scientist, who sang in his church choir. Fry was frustrated that the paper bookmarks he used to mark hymns kept slipping out of his hymnal. Recalling Silver's feeble adhesive, he applied some to slips of paper and found that they stayed in place yet could be removed without tearing the pages. The product that grew out of this idea, a pad of small notes with a strip of glue along one edge, went on sale across the United States in 1980 and soon became an office staple. The story is often told as a lesson in perseverance, but it also shows that an invention's value may lie in ____.

Long-distance travelers know the fog of jet lag, when a body that has crossed several time zones keeps insisting that it is still at home. Fewer realize that they may impose a milder version of the same condition on themselves every week. [A] Indeed, some airlines now offer lie-flat seats which allow long-haul passengers to sleep almost as comfortably as in a bed. [B] On workdays, alarm clocks force many people to wake hours earlier than their internal clocks would prefer, and they accumulate a sleep debt that they try to repay by sleeping late on weekends. [C] The resulting shift in sleep timing between weekdays and weekends has been labeled social jet lag, a term introduced by the chronobiologist Till Roenneberg. [D] Like ordinary jet lag, it leaves the body's internal rhythms out of step with the demands of daily life, so that on Monday mornings the alarm rings at what the body treats as the middle of the night. [E] Studies have associated larger gaps between weekday and weekend schedules with poorer mood, weaker academic performance, and a higher risk of obesity.
Researchers caution that much of this evidence is correlational, so it cannot prove that the shifting schedule itself causes the harm. Even so, many sleep scientists recommend keeping wake-up times fairly consistent across the week, and some argue that schools and employers should permit later starting times for those whose internal clocks run late.

The radio had not made a sound since my grandfather's funeral. It sat on a shelf in my mother's kitchen, a wooden box with a cracked dial and a smell of dust and old varnish, and none of us could bring ourselves to throw it away. One winter I resolved to repair it. I knew almost nothing about electronics, so I borrowed library books, watched tutorials late at night, and filled a notebook with diagrams I only half understood. Twice I replaced the wrong component. Once I gave myself a shock which left my fingers tingling for an hour.
In February, after I had cleaned the contacts and soldered a new capacitor into place, I switched it on. For a few seconds there was only a low hum. Then, faintly, came the voice of a weather forecaster announcing snow in the mountains. My mother, who had been washing dishes, stood motionless with her hands still in the water. Neither of us said anything. I had expected to feel proud, and I did, but what I felt more strongly was something closer to ____, as if a door I had assumed was locked forever had quietly swung open.

Attention is ____ rather than absolute: the brain sets most unattended sounds aside while continuing to monitor them for anything of personal importance. At a crowded party, dozens of conversations merge into a dull roar, yet most of us can follow the voice of the person in front of us with surprising ease. The British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry investigated this ability in 1953, coining the phrase the cocktail party problem. In his experiments, listeners wearing headphones heard a different message in each ear and were asked to repeat one of them aloud. They managed the task well but could report almost nothing about the other message; many failed to notice when it switched to a foreign language. Later research revealed, however, that the neglected channel is not entirely shut out. If one's own name is spoken in it, a substantial minority of listeners notice at once.

Learners of English are often bewildered that the letters in words such as bite, meet, and house seem to stand for sounds quite different from those the same letters represent in most European languages. The explanation lies largely in the Great Vowel Shift, a series of changes in pronunciation which unfolded roughly between 1400 and 1700. During this period, the long vowels of English migrated upward in the mouth; the vowel in bite, for instance, was once pronounced much like the vowel in modern beet. Unfortunately for later learners, the shift coincided with the arrival of printing, which encouraged printers and scholars to settle on standardized spellings. Many of those spellings reflected pronunciations that were already changing or would soon vanish. Consequently, the written language ____, preserving in its spelling a snapshot of how English sounded centuries ago. That is why modern English spelling often records the speech of the fifteenth century rather than that of today.

Sloths are often mocked as the laziest animals on Earth, but their sluggishness is better understood as an ingenious strategy. Their diet consists mainly of leaves, which are abundant but poor in nutrients and difficult to digest; a single meal can take days or even weeks to pass through a sloth's elaborate stomach. To survive on so little energy, sloths maintain a remarkably low metabolic rate, and their body temperature fluctuates with the surroundings more than in most mammals. They also carry comparatively little muscle, which reduces the energy required to sustain their bodies. Their slowness even offers protection. ____, predators such as harpy eagles and jaguars hunt largely by detecting movement, and a sloth hanging motionless high in the canopy, its fur tinged green by algae, is easily overlooked.

In 2023 Mexico overtook China as the largest source of goods imported into the United States, a milestone which reflected a broader rethinking of global supply chains. For decades, companies had chased the lowest production costs, often in East Asia, and accepted lengthy shipping routes as the price of cheap manufacturing. The pandemic exposed the fragility of that model: factory closures and port bottlenecks left shelves empty and assembly lines idle for months. Mounting tensions between Washington and Beijing, including tariffs on Chinese goods, added further incentive to diversify. Many firms have responded by relocating some production closer to their principal markets, a strategy known as nearshoring. Mexico, with its shared border, its trade agreement with the United States and Canada, and its experienced industrial workforce, has been an obvious beneficiary. Yet nearshoring has limits. Some Mexican factories still depend on components shipped from Asia, and shortages of electricity, water, and skilled engineers could constrain how quickly the shift proceeds.

Bottlenose dolphins live in fluid societies in which individuals constantly join and leave groups, so keeping track of one another is no trivial matter. [A] Within the first months of life, each dolphin develops a distinctive whistle, a contour of rising and falling pitch which differs from those of its companions. [B] Researchers call these signature whistles, because a dolphin broadcasts its own whistle much as a person announces a name, especially when separated from its group. [C] To test whether such copies really function as names, scientists played recordings to wild dolphins and found that the animals responded more strongly to imitations of their own signature than to the whistles of strangers. [D] Dolphins also appear to remember the whistles of former companions for many years; in one study, animals recognized the signatures of individuals they had not encountered for two decades. [E] Few other animals are known to use such learned vocal labels, which makes dolphins a valuable model for studying how names may have arisen.

In 1954 the American writer Sylvia Wright recounted a childhood memory in a magazine essay. [A] Her mother used to read aloud a Scottish ballad which included the line They have slain the Earl o' Moray, and laid him on the green. [B] Young Sylvia heard the last words as and Lady Mondegreen, and for years she pictured a tragic noblewoman perishing beside the earl. [C] Wright proposed calling such misheard phrases mondegreens, and the term has since entered dictionaries. [D] Mondegreens are especially common in song lyrics, where music blurs the boundaries between words and listeners cannot ask the singer to repeat a line. Psychologists find them revealing because they demonstrate that hearing is not a passive recording of sound. [E]

In 1929 a German psychologist showed people two drawings, one with rounded curves and the other with jagged points, and noticed something curious. [A] To find out whether the effect extended beyond European languages, researchers in 2001 repeated the test with American students and with speakers of Tamil in India, using the invented words bouba and kiki. [B] The vast majority in both groups paired bouba with the rounded figure, and the researchers concluded that such links between sounds and shapes may be universal. [C] Later researchers discovered that the story is more complicated. [D] In some communities the preference proved weak or absent, apparently because the invented words did not resemble possible words in the local language. [E] A listener for whom kiki sounds like nonsense may simply have no intuition about which figure it ought to name.

Today the Louvre in Paris is the most visited art museum in the world, but for most of its history it was not a museum at all.
(A) The building began in the late twelfth century as a fortress guarding the western edge of the city. Over the following centuries, French kings transformed it into a grand royal palace and filled it with paintings and sculptures.
(B) During the French Revolution, the new government seized the royal collections and declared that they belonged to the nation. In August 1793 the palace opened its doors as a public museum, admitting ordinary citizens to see works which had once been reserved for the court.
(C) That palace, however, gradually lost its central role after Louis XIV moved the court to Versailles in 1682. Artists and academies occupied many of its rooms, while the royal art collection remained largely hidden from public view.

Most people assume that a blood pressure reading taken in a doctor's office reflects their usual state. For many patients, however, the clinic itself raises the numbers, a phenomenon known as the white coat effect. [A] The mild anxiety of being examined can push readings well above the levels a patient maintains at home or at work. [B] In fact, the familiar inflatable cuff was devised in 1896 by the Italian physician Scipione Riva-Rocci, and its basic design has changed surprisingly little since then. [C] When patients wear portable monitors which record their blood pressure throughout an ordinary day, a substantial share of those diagnosed with hypertension in the clinic turn out to have normal readings elsewhere. [D] Such findings pose a dilemma for physicians, who must decide whether to prescribe drugs on the basis of numbers which may exaggerate the danger. [E] Many guidelines now recommend confirming high office readings with measurements taken outside the clinic before treatment begins, a practice which may spare patients unnecessary medication.

Until 1967 Sweden was an anomaly in continental Europe: its traffic kept to the left side of the road. [A] All of its neighbors drove on the right, and since most cars on Swedish roads had the steering wheel on the left, drivers overtaking on narrow roads had a poor view of oncoming traffic. [B] When the question was put to a referendum in 1955, however, more than four-fifths of voters rejected a change. [C] Parliament nevertheless approved the switch in 1963, citing rising traffic and the hazards facing drivers who crossed the border. [D] Moreover, Swedish manufacturers such as Volvo built a reputation for sturdy and safe automobiles which they retain to this day. [E] At ten minutes to five on the morning of September 3, 1967, all nonessential traffic halted, vehicles moved carefully to the opposite side of the road, and at five o'clock driving resumed on the right. Accidents actually fell in the following months, apparently because nervous drivers took unusual care, although the effect faded within a couple of years.

In October 2024, NASA launched Europa Clipper, the largest spacecraft the agency had ever built for a planetary mission, on a journey to Jupiter. Its target is Europa, one of Jupiter's many moons, a world slightly smaller than our own Moon whose icy crust is believed to conceal a global ocean of salty water. Because liquid water is considered essential for life as we know it, scientists regard Europa as one of the most promising places in the solar system to search for conditions which could sustain living organisms. The spacecraft will not land. Instead, after arriving in the Jupiter system in 2030, it will orbit the giant planet and swoop past Europa dozens of times, using cameras, radar, and other instruments to gauge the thickness of the ice, analyze the composition of the surface, and look for plumes of water vapor. To withstand Jupiter's intense radiation, its most sensitive electronics are housed inside a vault with thick metal walls. The mission is designed to determine whether Europa could be habitable, not to detect life itself.

Across Europe, the share of people registered as organ donors varies enormously between countries which seem otherwise similar. In some, fewer than a fifth of citizens are on the donor list; in neighboring countries with comparable cultures and health systems, nearly everyone is. An influential analysis published in 2003 traced much of this difference to a single administrative detail. Countries with very high rates used an opt-out system, in which citizens are presumed to consent unless they register an objection, whereas countries with low rates required people to actively opt in. Most people, it seems, simply accept whatever option is preset for them, whether out of inertia, uncertainty, or a sense that the default reflects an implicit recommendation. Policymakers have since exploited defaults deliberately, for instance by automatically enrolling employees in pension plans while allowing them to withdraw. Critics warn, however, that a box no one ticks is not the same as genuine consent, and that the actual number of transplants depends on many factors beyond the registry.

Every morning at the lost-property office on the airport's lower level, I unlock a storeroom which tells the story of the previous day's departures. There are always umbrellas, phone chargers, and paperback novels abandoned in seat pockets, but some items are harder to explain: a wedding dress, a set of dentures, once a live tortoise traveling in a shoebox. Last spring a man arrived breathless, three hours before his connecting flight, searching for a small blue notebook. He had left <u>it</u> on a bench by gate twelve, he said, and it held nothing valuable to anyone but him: the handwritten recipes of his late wife. We searched the shelves without success. Then a cleaner remembered finding a notebook in a cafe near the gate and handing it to a flight attendant. Forty minutes and several phone calls later, it was back in his hands. He said nothing for a moment; he simply opened it and turned the pages, one by one.

Why would anyone deliberately make success less likely? In a 1978 experiment, the psychologists Steven Berglas and Edward Jones gave students a set of problems and then told every one of them that they had performed very well. For some, the problems had been solvable; for others, they had been so difficult that the praise must have seemed baffling. Before a second test, the students were allowed to choose between two drugs, one described as improving performance and the other as impairing it. Students who had received unearned praise were far more likely to select the drug that would supposedly hurt their performance. The researchers called this strategy self-handicapping. By erecting an obstacle in advance, people secure a ready excuse if they fail, while any success appears all the more impressive. Everyday versions are familiar: the student who parties the night before an exam, or the athlete who skips practice before a big match. The protection is costly, however, because the handicap often brings about the very failure it was meant to explain away.

In 1967 the psychologists Edward Jones and Victor Harris asked American students to read essays which either praised or criticized Fidel Castro, then the leader of Cuba. Some readers were told that the writers had chosen their position freely; others were told that the writers had been assigned it, much like debaters told which side to argue. Remarkably, even readers who knew the position had been assigned concluded that the authors of pro-Castro essays genuinely admired him more than the others did. They gave too much weight to the writers' character and too little to the circumstances which had dictated what they wrote.
The psychologist Lee Ross later named this tendency the fundamental attribution error. It shows up everywhere. A driver who cuts us off seems reckless rather than late for a hospital; a colleague who misses a deadline seems lazy rather than overloaded. Curiously, we rarely judge ourselves so harshly, readily citing traffic or workload to explain our own lapses. Some cross-cultural studies suggest the bias is less ____ in societies that emphasize social roles and relationships, where people are more inclined to seek situational explanations of behavior. Recognizing the error does not abolish it, but pausing to ask what pressures another person might be facing can make our judgments fairer.

Marie Sklodowska grew up in Warsaw at a time when the Russian authorities who controlled the city barred women from attending university. [A] In 1891 she moved to Paris, enrolled at the Sorbonne, and lived for a time on so little money that she reportedly fainted from hunger during her studies. [B] There she met the physicist Pierre Curie, whom she married in 1895, and the couple began investigating the mysterious rays emitted by uranium. [C] Working in a drafty shed, they processed tons of mineral ore to isolate two new elements, which they named polonium, after Marie's homeland, and radium. [D] In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Henri Becquerel, becoming the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize. [E] After Pierre was killed in a street accident in 1906, she took over his professorship, and in 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, making her the first person honored in two scientific fields. She died in 1934 of a blood disorder which was very probably caused by decades of exposure to radiation.

Proteins are the molecular machines of living cells, and what each one does depends on the intricate three-dimensional shape into which its chain of amino acids folds. For half a century, determining those shapes was painstaking work. Researchers relied on techniques such as X-ray crystallography which could take months or years for a single protein, and predicting a structure from the amino acid sequence alone was regarded as one of biology's grand challenges.
In 2020 an artificial intelligence system called AlphaFold, developed by DeepMind, predicted protein structures with accuracy approaching that of laboratory methods. Its creators, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with David Baker, who had devised computational methods for designing entirely new proteins. AlphaFold's predictions for hundreds of millions of proteins have also been released in a public database, allowing scientists anywhere to examine structures within minutes. The tool is not infallible; its predictions are less reliable for proteins that change shape or lack a stable structure. ____, it has transformed how many laboratories begin their research, turning a question that once demanded years of experimental effort into a starting point.

In 1989, with smog in Mexico City among the worst of any major city, the government introduced a program called Hoy No Circula, meaning 'today it does not circulate.' Depending on the last digit of its license plate, each car was banned from the roads on one weekday. At first the policy appeared to work, as traffic thinned noticeably. Before long, however, many households responded by acquiring a second car, often an old and heavily polluting one, so that they would always have a vehicle permitted to drive. A later study found no evidence that air quality had improved and some evidence that the number of cars had grown. Economists now cite the program as a classic case of a regulation which produces the ____ of its intended result, as when a rule designed to curb pollution ends up encouraging people to buy dirtier cars. The episode serves as a reminder that people respond to rules in ways that planners rarely foresee.

Beriberi, a disease caused by a lack of vitamin B1, ravaged the Japanese navy in the late nineteenth century, when sailors lived largely on polished white rice. In 1883 the training ship Ryujo returned from a nine-month voyage with nearly half of its crew stricken and twenty-five dead. Takaki Kanehiro, a naval surgeon trained in London, persuaded the navy to send another ship, the Tsukuba, along the same route the following year with a diet richer in meat, barley, and vegetables. Only a handful of men fell ill. The voyage is often celebrated as an early (A) ____ experiment in nutrition, because the two voyages differed chiefly in what the crews ate. Yet its lesson was not universally heeded. Takaki wrongly blamed a lack of protein, and the army, unconvinced, kept feeding its soldiers white rice for years. The (B) ____ in adopting a proven remedy cost countless soldiers their health.

____ Before the eleventh century, singers in European monasteries learned the chants of the liturgy almost entirely by ear, a process which could take a decade of patient repetition. Written signs placed above the words reminded singers of the general contour of a melody but did not indicate exact pitches. The Italian monk Guido of Arezzo devised a system of horizontal lines on which notes could be placed to show precisely how high or low each should be sung, the ancestor of the modern staff. He also taught pupils to associate pitches with the opening syllables of each line of a familiar hymn, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, a method which survives in the singing exercises still used today. Guido boasted that with his techniques a boy could master in a few months what had previously required years.

Vervet monkeys, small primates which live in the savannas and woodlands of eastern and southern Africa, face danger from several very different predators. In the late 1970s researchers working in Kenya documented that the monkeys give distinct alarm calls for leopards, eagles, and snakes, and that each call triggers a fitting response. On hearing the leopard call, monkeys dash up into the trees; the eagle call sends them looking skyward or diving into bushes; the snake call makes them rise on their hind legs and scan the grass. Their reactions were not merely responses to the caller's agitation. When the researchers played recorded calls from hidden loudspeakers, with no predator in sight, the monkeys still reacted appropriately to each one. Such findings have prompted scholars to reconsider the long-held assumption that signals referring to specific things in the world were ____ to our own species. Some now regard these calls as a glimpse of the evolutionary roots of meaning.

Hedy Lamarr was one of the most famous film stars of the 1940s, promoted in Hollywood publicity as the most beautiful woman in the world. Few of her admirers knew that she devoted her spare hours to inventing. During the Second World War, worried that radio-controlled torpedoes could easily be jammed by the enemy, she and the composer George Antheil devised a method in which the transmitter and receiver would switch rapidly among many frequencies in a synchronized pattern, making the signal extremely difficult to intercept or disrupt. Antheil, who had once synchronized player pianos in an avant-garde composition, suggested a mechanism similar to a piano roll. The pair received a patent in 1942, but the United States Navy did not adopt the idea during the war, and Lamarr earned nothing from it. Decades later, frequency-hopping techniques became part of the foundation of secure military communications and, eventually, of technologies related to Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Lamarr received public recognition for her invention only late in life.

The Hungarian-American psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi spent years asking people to describe the moments when they felt most fully alive.
(A) This balance helps explain why flow is not a fixed reward. As skill grows, the same task becomes dull, so people must keep seeking slightly greater challenges to recapture the experience, a cycle which drives them to keep improving.
(B) He also identified the conditions under which it tends to arise. The activity must have clear goals and immediate feedback, and, crucially, its challenge must match the person's skill. A task that is too easy breeds boredom; one that is too hard breeds anxiety.
(C) Surgeons, rock climbers, chess players, and painters gave strikingly similar answers. They spoke of becoming so absorbed in an activity that time seemed to vanish and self-consciousness dropped away. Csikszentmihalyi called this state flow.

More than a tenth of world trade normally passes through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, the shortest sea route between Asia and Europe. [A] Beginning in late 2023, however, Houthi militants in Yemen launched missiles and drones at commercial ships in the region, describing the attacks as a response to the war in Gaza. [B] Major shipping lines responded by diverting vessels around the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa. [C] The detour added roughly ten days to a typical voyage between Asia and northern Europe, along with millions of dollars in extra fuel costs. [D] Freight rates rose sharply, and some European factories briefly halted production while awaiting delayed components. [E] Egypt, which depends heavily on canal fees as a source of foreign currency, saw its revenue from the waterway plummet.

For most of history, the length of a second was defined by the rotation of the Earth: one day divided into 86,400 equal parts. [A] Since 1967, however, the official second has been based on the vibrations of cesium atoms, which are far more regular than the planet's spin. [B] The Earth's rotation varies slightly from year to year, influenced by tides, earthquakes, and the movement of its molten core. [C] To keep the two in step, timekeepers began in 1972 to insert an occasional leap second into Coordinated Universal Time. [D] These insertions created headaches for computer networks, some of which crashed or malfunctioned when a minute suddenly contained sixty-one seconds. [E] In 2022, international metrologists voted to stop adding leap seconds by 2035, accepting that atomic time and the Earth's rotation will gradually drift apart.

In the 1990s the United States government launched one of the most ambitious social experiments in its history, known as Moving to Opportunity. [A] Notably, Americans have historically changed their place of residence more often than people in most other wealthy countries. [B] Several thousand low-income families living in public housing in five large cities were selected by lottery, and some received vouchers which helped them rent homes in neighborhoods with far less poverty. [C] Their outcomes were then compared with those of families who had not received the vouchers. [D] The early results disappointed those who had anticipated a large rise in earnings: adults who moved earned little more than those who stayed. [E] They did, however, report better mental health and were less likely to suffer from extreme obesity and diabetes, findings that supporters cite as evidence that place itself shapes well-being. Later analyses found that children who moved while young went on to earn substantially more as adults.

The Arctic tern, a slender seabird weighing little more than a hundred grams, makes the longest known migration of any animal. [A] Each year it breeds in the Arctic during the northern summer and then flies to the edge of Antarctica for the southern summer, so that it probably experiences more daylight than any other creature. [B] Tracking devices small enough to attach to the birds have revealed that their routes are far from direct; many zigzag across the Atlantic to exploit favorable winds and rich feeding areas. [C] As a result, a single tern may travel more than seventy thousand kilometers in a year. [D] Penguins, which cannot fly, are the best-known birds of the Antarctic and rely on thick layers of fat to survive the cold. [E] Because terns can live for thirty years, an individual may cover a distance over its lifetime equivalent to three round trips to the Moon.

Why does a walk in a park leave many people feeling mentally refreshed? In the 1980s, the psychologists Rachel and Stephen Kaplan proposed an explanation known as attention restoration theory. Much of modern life, they argued, <u>demands</u> directed attention: we must deliberately focus on traffic, screens, and conversations while suppressing distractions, and this effortful capacity becomes <u>depleted</u> with use. Natural settings, by contrast, engage a gentler kind of attention. Rustling leaves, drifting clouds, and flowing water hold our interest <u>effortlessly</u>, giving the mechanisms of deliberate focus a chance to recover. Some experiments support the idea: participants who walked through an arboretum performed <u>worse</u> afterward on a demanding memory task than those who walked along busy city streets. The theory has practical implications for urban planning, suggesting that parks and street trees are not mere decoration but resources for mental health. Accordingly, many planners now treat green space as a <u>necessity</u> rather than a luxury.

Imagine summoning an air taxi which lifts off from a rooftop, glides over traffic jams, and sets you down across the city in minutes. Dozens of companies are racing to make this vision, often called urban air mobility, a reality. Most are developing electric aircraft capable of vertical takeoff and landing, which use multiple small rotors rather than a single large one. Battery power promises quieter and cleaner flight than helicopters, and simpler electric motors could reduce maintenance costs. Formidable obstacles remain, however. Batteries are heavy relative to the energy they store, limiting how far the aircraft can fly and how many passengers they can carry. Regulators must certify an entirely new category of aircraft and devise rules for managing dense low-altitude traffic over cities. Cities, in turn, will need landing sites, known as vertiports, equipped with chargers and space for passengers. Above all, the industry must persuade the public that small aircraft buzzing over homes are safe and tolerably quiet. Several companies have already postponed their planned launch dates more than once.

Graduates, I know that some of you are leaving today with a job offer in your pocket and a clear plan for the next ten years. I also know that many of you have no idea what comes next, and that this uncertainty feels like failure on a day meant for celebration. Let me tell you something I wish someone had told me when I sat where you are sitting. My first job after university lasted four months. My second involved selling encyclopedias door to door, which tells you how long ago that was. It took me nearly a decade to find work I loved, and every detour along the way taught me something I still use. The people I admire most did not follow straight lines. They followed their curiosity, tolerated confusion, and kept learning. So if you feel lost today, you are in excellent company. Be patient with yourselves. The path will reveal itself, but only to those who keep walking.

On the night of August 21, 1986, the residents of several villages near Lake Nyos, a crater lake in northwestern Cameroon, went to sleep without any sign of danger. By morning, about 1,700 people and thousands of cattle lay dead, many of them in their beds, yet there had been no fire, no flood, and no visible explosion. Investigators soon pieced together what had happened. Carbon dioxide seeping from volcanic rock beneath the lake had been dissolving for years in its deep, cold water, held there by the pressure above like the gas in a sealed bottle of soda. Something, perhaps a landslide, disturbed the layers, and the gas burst out of solution all at once. Because carbon dioxide is heavier than air, the invisible cloud rolled down the valleys and suffocated nearly everyone in its path. Since 2001, pipes inserted into the lake have slowly vented the gas from its depths so that such a catastrophe should not recur.

In 1945 Percy Spencer, a self-taught engineer at the American defense company Raytheon, was working near a magnetron, a device which generated the microwaves used in military radar. According to the often-repeated account, he noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted, even though he felt no heat himself. Curious, he placed popcorn kernels near the device and watched them burst; an egg he tested next reportedly exploded. Spencer realized that microwaves could heat food by making the water molecules inside it vibrate rapidly.
Raytheon patented the idea and in 1947 introduced the first commercial microwave oven. It stood nearly as tall as a person, weighed hundreds of kilograms, and cost thousands of dollars, so its early buyers were restaurants, ships, and railway companies rather than households. Decades of engineering were needed to make the device smaller, cheaper, and safer before it became a fixture in ordinary kitchens. The story is a reminder that a chance observation becomes an invention only when ____.

In many countries, tipping is limited to a few occasions, but in the United States it has long been woven into the economics of service work. [A] Under federal law, restaurants may pay tipped employees a cash wage far below the standard minimum wage, provided that tips bring their earnings up to at least the minimum. [B] In recent years, however, requests for tips have spread well beyond restaurants. [C] The practice of tipping is believed to have originated in Tudor England, where guests at aristocratic estates gave small sums to their hosts' servants. [D] Digital payment screens at coffee shops, bakeries, and even self-service kiosks now routinely suggest gratuities of fifteen, twenty, or twenty-five percent, often for transactions involving little personal service. [E] Many customers report feeling pressured by these prompts, particularly when an employee is watching them choose.
Surveys suggest mounting irritation, a phenomenon some commentators have dubbed tip fatigue. Defenders of tipping argue that it rewards good service and supplements low wages, but critics contend that it shifts the responsibility for paying workers from employers to customers and makes earnings unpredictable. Some restaurants have experimented with abolishing tips in favor of higher menu prices and fixed wages, with mixed results.

The pilot boat pitched in the black swell as we drew alongside the container ship, a wall of steel rising higher than a ten-story building. Somewhere above, a rope ladder dangled against the hull, swinging with each roll of the vessel. Captain Ruiz, who had been guiding ships into this harbor for twenty-two years, zipped up his jacket, waited for the boat to rise on a wave, and stepped onto the ladder as casually as a man boarding a bus. I was there to learn the job, and my stomach lurched as I watched him climb.
On the bridge, he greeted the vessel's commander, studied the radar, and began issuing quiet instructions to the helmsman. For the next two hours he brought the enormous vessel through a narrow channel, past sandbanks and anchored tankers, without once raising his voice. Later I asked how he stayed so calm. He shrugged. The ladder was the only dangerous part, he said; everything else was simply knowing the harbor better than anyone on board. I realized then that his composure was not a matter of temperament but of ____, built from thousands of nights spent learning every bend and shoal of the channel.

Musicians and athletes who falter under pressure are often not lacking in skill; their arousal has simply become ____. In 1908 the psychologists Robert Yerkes and John Dodson reported an experiment in which mice learned to choose between two compartments, receiving electric shocks of varying strength whenever they entered the wrong one. Somewhat counterintuitively, the mice learned fastest not with the weakest or the strongest shocks but with those of intermediate intensity, at least when the discrimination was difficult. Later psychologists extrapolated this finding into a principle which now bears their names. Up to a point, stress and arousal heighten vigilance and improve performance; a little anxiety before an exam can motivate careful preparation. Beyond that point, however, performance begins to deteriorate, as intrusive rumination and physical tension crowd out lucid thinking. The ideal level also varies with the task. Simple, well-rehearsed activities tolerate high arousal, whereas intricate ones suffer sooner.

Since 1982, a row of burnished steel gates has spanned the River Thames downstream of central London. Most of the time the Thames Barrier lies open, its rotating gates resting flat on the riverbed so that ships can pass freely. When forecasters predict an unusually high tide combined with a storm surge from the North Sea, the gates are swung upward to form a continuous wall, shielding low-lying districts of the city from inundation. The barrier was built after a catastrophic North Sea flood in 1953 killed hundreds of people along England's east coast and exposed how vulnerable the capital was. It was originally expected to provide protection until around 2030, but assiduous maintenance has extended its anticipated life. As sea levels rise, the gates are likely to be closed ever more often. In effect, a structure designed for rare emergencies may gradually become ____. The barrier already closes far more often in a typical year than it did in its first decade of service.

The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, who ruled from 161 to 180 CE, spent much of his reign on military campaigns along the empire's northern frontier. In the evenings, he wrote private notes to himself in Greek, reminding himself to remain patient, to accept what lay beyond his control, and to treat even difficult people with fairness. These notes, now known as the Meditations, were never intended for publication. ____, they have become one of the most widely read works of ancient philosophy, although they read less like a treatise than like a conversation a man conducts with his own conscience, replete with repetitions, admonitions, and self-corrections. That intimacy may explain their enduring appeal. Readers who would never open a systematic work of philosophy find in them the voice of a powerful man struggling, as ordinary people do, to live up to his own ideals.

For most travelers, the airport where they change planes is little more than a place to rush between gates. For the cities which host them, however, major transfer hubs are coveted economic assets. Airlines concentrate their networks at a hub so that passengers from dozens of smaller cities can connect to hundreds of destinations, an arrangement known as the hub-and-spoke system. The more connections a hub offers, the more passengers it attracts, and the more passengers it attracts, the more routes become profitable. This self-perpetuating cycle has fueled intense rivalry. Dubai, Doha, and Istanbul have invested colossal sums in vast terminals and state-backed airlines, positioning themselves as natural stopping points between Europe, Asia, and Africa. Older hubs have responded with new runways and faster transfer procedures, and Incheon in South Korea has promoted itself with expeditious connections and amenities designed for long layovers. Yet the competition rests on a precarious foundation. New long-range aircraft can fly many routes directly, allowing travelers to bypass hubs altogether.

The hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain, plays a pivotal role in consolidating new memories, and in most adults it gradually shrinks with age. [A] For a long time this decline was regarded as an inevitable feature of growing old. [B] In a widely cited study published in 2011, however, researchers randomly assigned about 120 older adults either to a program of brisk walking three times a week or to a program of stretching and toning exercises. [C] Interestingly, seahorses are unusual among fish because the males, rather than the females, carry the developing young. [D] After a year, the hippocampus had grown by roughly two percent in the walking group, while it had continued to shrink in the stretching group. [E] The walkers also showed modest improvements in spatial memory, suggesting that aerobic exercise may help preserve the aging brain. The researchers caution that exercise is no guarantee against dementia, but the findings offer a compelling reason to keep moving.

In the Republic, Plato asks his readers to envisage prisoners who have spent their entire lives shackled inside a cave, facing a blank wall. [A] Behind them burns a fire, and between the fire and the prisoners people carry objects whose shadows fall on the wall. [B] Knowing nothing else, the prisoners mistake the flickering silhouettes for reality itself. [C] If one of them were freed and dragged into the sunlight, he would at first be dazzled and disoriented, and only gradually would his eyes adjust to the luminous world outside. [D] Returning to the cave to free the others, he would find his eyes unaccustomed to the darkness, and his former companions would deride him and obstinately resist his efforts. [E] Indeed, many caves around the world contain prehistoric paintings, some created more than thirty thousand years ago. The allegory has been read as a portrait of education, which Plato saw not as filling an empty vessel but as turning the soul toward the light.

Lightning has terrified people for as long as there have been storms, and for centuries church towers, the tallest buildings in most towns, bore the brunt of it. [A] In the early 1750s Benjamin Franklin proposed a safeguard: a pointed iron rod fixed to the top of a building and connected by a wire to the ground. [B] Contrary to a widespread belief, such a rod does not draw lightning toward a building or prevent strikes altogether. [C] What it does is offer the current a safe path, carrying it harmlessly into the earth instead of letting it pass through timber and masonry, where it can ignite conflagrations or fracture walls. [D] Some clergy initially protested that the devices interfered with the will of God, but the steady decline in damage to protected buildings proved decisive. [E] Today lightning protection systems built on Franklin's principle guard everything from skyscrapers to wind turbines.

In 2007 a young real estate agent named John Maloof bought a box of old negatives at a Chicago auction, hoping to find pictures for a local history book. [A] Instead he found thousands of extraordinary street photographs taken from the 1950s onward: shoppers, children, laborers, and strangers caught in evanescent moments of humor and sorrow. [B] The photographer was Vivian Maier, a woman who had worked for decades as a nanny for families in Chicago and New York. [C] She had taken well over a hundred thousand pictures but showed them to almost no one, and many of her rolls of film had never even been developed. [D] When Maloof posted some of the images online, they attracted enormous attention, and exhibitions and a documentary film soon followed. [E] Today Maier is counted among the notable street photographers of the twentieth century, although disputes persist over who should profit from work she never chose to publish.

Until the middle of the twentieth century, there was no standardized way to appraise the condition of a newborn baby in the first moments of life. [A] In 1952 Virginia Apgar, an American anesthesiologist, devised a rudimentary score to fill that gap. [B] One minute after birth, a doctor or nurse rates the baby from zero to two on each of five signs: heart rate, breathing, muscle tone, reflex response, and skin color. [C] A total of seven or above is generally reassuring, while a low score signals that the infant may need immediate help, and the assessment is usually repeated at five minutes. [D] The method was quick enough to use in a frenetic delivery room and required no specialized apparatus. [E] Within a decade it was being used in hospitals across the United States, and it remains a ubiquitous part of neonatal care around the world.

In the early nineteenth century, a Cherokee silversmith named Sequoyah became persuaded that the written words of white Americans, which he called talking leaves, gave them a formidable advantage.
(A) Although he could not read any language, he set out to create a writing system for his own people. After experimenting fruitlessly with a separate symbol for every word, he realized that the language could be broken down into a limited number of syllables.
(B) He assigned a symbol to each of them, eventually arriving at a set of eighty-six characters. In 1821, after his young daughter demonstrated that she could read his messages, Cherokee leaders formally endorsed the system.
(C) What followed was astounding. Because learners needed to memorize only the symbols, many Cherokee became literate within months, and in 1828 the first newspaper in a Native American language, the Cherokee Phoenix, began publication.

On October 13, 2024, SpaceX accomplished a feat which many engineers had considered close to impossible. During the fifth test flight of its Starship system, the enormous Super Heavy booster, after lifting the upper stage toward space, turned back toward its launch site in Texas. Instead of landing on legs or plunging into the sea, it slowed its descent with its engines and was caught in midair by two giant mechanical arms mounted on the launch tower. Meanwhile, the Starship upper stage flew on and later made a controlled splashdown in the Indian Ocean. Catching the booster is meant to allow it to be refueled and launched again quickly, and a vehicle without landing legs is lighter and can carry more cargo. Reusability is pivotal to the company's strategy for lowering the cost of reaching orbit. Critics, however, point to the environmental impact of frequent launches and to debris strewn by earlier test vehicles which exploded.

A considerable share of the fruit and vegetables grown on farms never reaches a shop shelf, and not because it is spoiled or unsafe. Supermarkets have long imposed stringent cosmetic standards on produce, rejecting forked carrots, blemished apples, or overly curved cucumbers. Shoppers, accustomed to immaculate displays, have come to expect uniformity, and retailers fear that oddly shaped items will remain unsold. As a result, perfectly edible produce is often plowed back into the soil, fed to animals, or discarded. In recent years, campaigns against food waste have attempted to rehabilitate so-called ugly produce. Some retailers sell misshapen fruit and vegetables at a discount, and delivery services offer boxes of imperfect items directly to households. These efforts have had some success, but critics point out that they tackle just one part of the problem, because a large share of the food wasted in wealthy countries is thrown away not on farms but in homes.

Few mammals are as superbly adapted to frigid conditions as the Arctic fox. Its thick winter fur, which covers even the soles of its feet, provides such effective insulation that the animal does not begin to shiver until the temperature falls far below zero.
