Its short legs, small ears, and rounded body minimize the surface area through which heat can dissipate. The fox's coat also changes with the seasons. In many populations, the dense white fur of winter is molted in spring and replaced by a thinner brown or gray coat. The change is not merely a matter of temperature. Against snow, a white coat camouflages the fox from the rodents it stalks and from larger predators; once the snow melts, a white animal would stand out conspicuously against rocks and tundra, while a darker coat blends into the summer landscape. Some populations, particularly along coasts, remain a smoky bluish gray throughout the year.

Gyms tend to fill up in January, and resolutions to eat better or save more money coalesce around the start of a new year. Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania wondered whether the calendar itself shapes such efforts. Analyzing gym attendance records and internet searches for the word diet, Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman, and Jason Riis found that interest in self-improvement rose not only on New Year's Day but also at the start of each week and month, after public holidays, and following birthdays. They called this pattern the fresh start effect. Such dates, they suggested, act as psychological dividing lines, allowing people to separate their present selves from past failures and to feel that a new chapter has begun. The insight has practical applications. Reminders to begin a savings plan or a health program may be more persuasive when they are tied to an upcoming landmark, such as the first day of spring, than when they arrive on an ordinary Wednesday.

For centuries, nostalgia was regarded as a disorder. The word was coined in 1688 by a Swiss medical student, Johannes Hofer, who combined the Greek words for homecoming and pain to describe the debilitating homesickness he observed among soldiers serving far from home. Physicians of later generations blamed it on everything from brain disease to the incessant clanging of cowbells in the Alps. [A] Today, many psychologists take a far more favorable view. [B] Research led by Constantine Sedikides and his colleagues suggests that nostalgia, a sentimental longing for the past, is a common and largely positive emotion. [C] People tend to become nostalgic when they feel lonely, anxious, or adrift, and recalling cherished memories appears to restore a sense of meaning and connection. [D] In experiments, participants asked to recall a nostalgic event subsequently reported higher self-esteem and felt more socially supported than those who recalled an ordinary event. [E] Some studies even suggest that nostalgia can make people feel physically warmer on a chilly day. Nostalgia, in this view, is less a sickness than a resource.

When the United States began sending astronauts into orbit, the precise paths of their spacecraft were calculated not only by electronic computers but also by people. Katherine Johnson, an African American mathematician, joined the agency which became NASA in 1953 as one of a group of women employed as human computers. At first she worked in a segregated unit at the Langley laboratory in Virginia, where Black employees were required to use separate dining and restroom facilities.
Her skill soon made her indispensable. She calculated the trajectory for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight, the first by an American in space, and before John Glenn's orbital flight in 1962 he reportedly insisted that she personally verify the figures produced by the new electronic computers. If she said the numbers were good, he declared, he was ready to go. Despite such trust, her contributions remained largely ____ to the public for decades. Only late in life did recognition arrive: in 2015 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and a popular film released in 2016 brought her story to a wide audience. She died in 2020 at the age of 101.

Meat grown from animal cells in large steel tanks, without raising or slaughtering livestock, has migrated from speculative fiction to restaurant menus in only a few years. [A] In 2020 Singapore became the first country to approve the sale of cultivated chicken, and in 2023 regulators in the United States cleared two companies to sell similar products. [B] After all, chicken is among the most widely eaten meats in the world, and global consumption has risen steadily for decades. [C] Supporters argue that cultivated meat could eventually reduce the land, water, and greenhouse gas emissions associated with livestock farming, as well as the suffering of sentient animals. [D] The technology has also provoked a backlash. In 2023 Italy passed a law banning the production and sale of cultivated meat, and in 2024 Florida and Alabama adopted similar bans, invoking the protection of ranchers and traditional food culture. [E] Skeptics also note that producing cultivated meat at scale remains prohibitively expensive and that its environmental benefits depend heavily on the energy used to power production. For now, the products remain scarce, available only in a handful of restaurants.

In a continent dominated by a single family of related tongues, Basque remains a genuine ____. Spoken by several hundred thousand people in a region straddling the border between Spain and France, Basque stands apart from every other language in Western Europe. Nearly all of its neighbors, from Spanish and French to English and German, belong to the Indo-European family and share ancestral roots which can be traced through regular sound changes. Basque does not. Linguists have proposed links to languages as distant as Georgian, but none of these theories has won general acceptance, and most scholars classify it as a language isolate. Its survival is remarkable. Basque appears to predate the arrival of Indo-European languages in the region, outlasted centuries of Roman rule, and weathered periods in the twentieth century when its public use was restricted. Today it is taught in schools and broadcast on television.

Antarctic krill, shrimp-like crustaceans rarely longer than a person's finger, may be the most abundant wild animal on Earth by total weight. They gather in swarms so dense that they can tint the sea pink, and they constitute the foundation of a food web that sustains whales, seals, penguins, and fish. Their importance extends beyond feeding other animals. Krill graze on microscopic algae near the surface and excrete compact fecal pellets which plummet into the deep ocean, carrying carbon with them. In this way, these tiny animals play a (A) ____ role in removing carbon from the atmosphere and storing it far below the surface. Scientists are therefore concerned about pressures on krill populations, including the loss of the sea ice under which young krill shelter in winter and a growing fishery that harvests them for fish feed and dietary supplements. Protecting krill, they argue, is not a (B) ____ matter for specialists but a question with consequences for the climate of the entire planet.

During the 1960s, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman was lecturing flight instructors in the Israeli air force on the virtues of praise when one veteran objected. Whenever he commended a cadet for an exceptionally smooth maneuver, he said, the next attempt was usually worse; whenever he berated a cadet for a clumsy one, the next attempt generally improved. Punishment, he concluded, was more efficacious than praise. Kahneman recognized a statistical illusion. Any single performance reflects both skill and a considerable dose of chance, so an extraordinarily good or bad attempt is likely to be followed by one closer to the pilot's habitual level, whatever the instructor says. Statisticians call this regression to the mean. The phenomenon is ubiquitous and frequently misattributed: a patient who seeks treatment at the peak of an ailment often recovers regardless of the remedy. Before crediting any intervention, therefore, one should ask whether the change would have occurred ____. Many a remedy owes its reputation to patients who would have recovered anyway.

For most of the twentieth century, urban planning assumed that cities would keep growing. Detroit, for instance, burgeoned to nearly two million residents by 1950 as the automobile industry flourished. Over the following decades, however, factory jobs disappeared and many families moved to the suburbs or to other regions, and by 2020 the city's population had fallen to roughly 640,000. Detroit is not unique; many industrial cities in Europe and Asia have also lost large numbers of residents. Depopulation presents problems which growth-oriented planning never anticipated: derelict houses, schools without pupils, and streets and pipes that must be maintained for far fewer taxpayers. ____, some cities have begun to treat decline as something to manage rather than reverse, demolishing abandoned buildings, converting empty lots into gardens and parks, and concentrating services in the neighborhoods which remain densely populated.

The Tour de France, now one of the world's most famous sporting events, began as a promotional gimmick. In 1903 the French sports newspaper L'Auto was locked in a fierce circulation battle with a rival publication. One of its journalists proposed a bicycle race around the country, and the editor, Henri Desgrange, seized on the scheme, hoping that daily reports of the riders' ordeal would boost sales. The first race covered roughly 2,400 kilometers in six grueling stages, some of which continued through the night over rough roads. Only about a third of the sixty riders who started managed to finish. The gamble proved lucrative: L'Auto's circulation soared, and its rival soon went out of business. The race also left a lasting mark on cycling's traditions. The yellow jersey awarded to the overall leader, introduced in 1919, was chosen to match the yellow paper on which L'Auto was printed.

Many people possess skills their neighbors could use: one can fix a leaking tap, another can tutor a child in arithmetic, a third can drive an elderly resident to the doctor.
(A) Members earn one credit for every hour they spend helping someone else and can redeem it for an hour of help from any other member, whatever the task. Many such banks also hold regular gatherings at which members meet and swap requests.
(B) Some communities have tried to put these idle talents to work by creating time banks, which trade hours of service instead of money. Volunteers or local charities often run these networks.
(C) Supporters argue that such exchanges help people on low incomes obtain services they could not otherwise afford. The regular gatherings may also ease loneliness, since participants exchange companionship along with favors.

In the 1970s and 1980s, acid rain became one of the most alarming environmental scourges in North America and Europe. [A] Sulfur dioxide released by coal-burning power plants combined with moisture in the atmosphere to form acids, which fell as rain and snow, defoliating forests and leaving lakes too acidic for fish. [B] In 1990 the United States adopted an innovative remedy. [C] Rather than prescribing how each plant should curtail emissions, the government set a national limit on total sulfur dioxide and issued tradable permits, allowing companies that could reduce pollution cheaply to sell their surplus allowances to those for whom cuts were costly. [D] Coal was also the fuel which powered the steam engines of the Industrial Revolution in nineteenth-century Britain. [E] The program curtailed emissions faster and at lower cost than many had predicted, and it became a model for later proposals to limit carbon dioxide through similar cap-and-trade systems.

With its body covered in overlapping scales, the pangolin looks more like a walking pine cone than a mammal. [A] Pine trees produce cones which open in dry weather to release their seeds. [B] The scales are made of keratin, the same protein found in human fingernails, and when threatened the animal curls into a tight ball which even a lion struggles to pry open. [C] Pangolins have no teeth; instead they use powerful claws to tear into ant and termite nests and a long, sticky tongue to gather the insects inside. [D] Sadly, the armor which protects them from predators offers no defense against people. [E] Pangolins are believed to be among the most heavily trafficked wild mammals in the world, hunted for their meat and for scales used in traditional remedies, and all eight species are now protected under international trade rules.

In 2007 the African Union launched an ambitious project known as the Great Green Wall. [A] The plan was to plant a band of trees roughly eight thousand kilometers long across the southern edge of the Sahara, from Senegal in the west to Djibouti in the east, to halt the advance of the desert. [B] Progress proved far slower than its founders had hoped. [C] These difficulties were compounded by the loss of many early seedlings, which had been placed in harsh soils without the care and water they needed. [D] Over time, the project's emphasis shifted from planting a literal wall of trees to restoring degraded land in many forms, including helping farmers protect the young trees which sprout naturally in their fields. [E] Supporters argue that this approach, which treats local communities as partners rather than laborers, is far more likely to endure.

Most fish suffocate within minutes on dry land, but the mudskipper spends much of its life out of the water. [A] Found on tidal mudflats and in mangrove swamps from Africa to Australia, it hops and crawls across the mud on robust pectoral fins, chasing insects and small crabs at low tide. [B] The fish can absorb oxygen through its skin and the lining of its mouth, provided that these surfaces remain moist. [C] It also carries a supply of water in enlarged gill chambers, much as a diver carries air. [D] To stay damp, it rolls in puddles from time to time, and when the tide returns it retreats into a burrow it has dug in the mud. [E] This remarkable parental behavior, together with the fish's amphibious habits, is one reason biologists study mudskippers for clues to how the first vertebrates may have made the transition from water to land hundreds of millions of years ago.

Desk jobs, long commutes, and evenings in front of screens leave many adults sedentary for most of the day. Epidemiologists have linked prolonged sitting to a <u>higher</u> risk of heart disease, diabetes, and premature death, and some studies suggest that these risks are <u>reduced</u> only partly by regular exercise. In other words, an hour at the gym may not fully <u>offset</u> an entire day spent in a chair. One explanation is that muscles that remain inactive for long periods use <u>more</u> glucose and fat, allowing these substances to accumulate in the blood. Standing desks have proliferated as a result, but standing still for hours brings ailments of its own, such as lumbar and foot pain. Most experts therefore recommend alternating one's posture and taking short walking breaks every half hour or so. The key, it seems, is not any particular position but <u>frequent</u> movement.

Inside many modern warehouses, the shelves come to the workers rather than the other way around. Squat wheeled robots slide beneath tall storage racks, lift them, and carry them to stations where human employees pick the items needed for each order. Other machines sort parcels, unload trucks, or glide autonomously along the aisles carrying plastic totes. The surge in online shopping has accelerated this trend, since retailers face pressure to deliver huge volumes of goods quickly while labor is scarce and costly. Robots excel at monotonous, repetitive movement, but many tasks remain difficult for them. Grasping objects of heterogeneous shape, softness, and size, from a bag of rice to a glass bottle, still challenges even advanced robotic arms, which is why picking is often the last step to be automated. Companies argue that robots relieve workers of exhausting walking and heavy lifting, while labor advocates warn that the machines can intensify the pace of work for those who remain and reduce the number of jobs over time.

The painting arrived in my studio last autumn wrapped in blankets, its surface dulled by a century of candle smoke and a thick layer of yellowed varnish. Before intervening, I spent two weeks scrutinizing it under ultraviolet light and magnification, documenting every earlier restoration. Someone in the 1950s had overpainted a damaged corner with a blue which did not quite harmonize with the sky. My first task was to remove the old varnish, working with small cotton swabs and solvents tested on an inconspicuous patch no larger than a fingernail. Progress was painstaking, measured in square centimeters per day. As the grime dissolved, colors which no one living had seen emerged: a pale green in the distant hills, a red scarf on a figure I had assumed was wearing brown. The rule I follow is simple. Everything I add must be reversible, so that a future specialist can undo my work if superior methods emerge.

In 1888, when his brother Ludvig died, Alfred Nobel reportedly opened a French newspaper to find his own obituary. The paper had confused the two brothers, and, according to the often-repeated story, it described Alfred, the inventor of dynamite, as a merchant of death who had grown rich by finding ways to kill more people faster. Whether or not the episode happened exactly this way, Nobel became increasingly preoccupied with how he would be remembered. In his final will, signed in 1895, he left most of his immense fortune to establish prizes for those who had conferred the greatest benefit on humankind in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and the promotion of peace between nations. His relatives contested the will, and it took several years to settle the estate. The first prizes were awarded in 1901, five years after his death. A fortune built largely on explosives thus came to fund the most prestigious honors in science and letters.

In 1970 Soviet scientists began drilling into the Kola Peninsula, near the border with Norway, with an audacious goal: to penetrate as deeply as possible into the Earth's crust. The project continued for roughly two decades. By 1989 the borehole had reached a depth of about 12,262 meters, making it the deepest artificial hole on Earth, a record it still holds. Yet that depth amounts to only about a third of the way through the continental crust in that region, a reminder of how little of the planet's interior humans have directly sampled.
The drilling yielded several surprises. Rock temperatures at the bottom reached about 180 degrees Celsius, far hotter than expected, and the heat made the rock behave almost like plastic, causing the drill to become stuck repeatedly. Scientists also found water deep underground, trapped in the rock where few had expected it, and discovered microscopic fossils of plankton several kilometers below the surface. When funding dried up after the collapse of the Soviet Union, the project was abandoned, and the hole was eventually sealed with a metal cap. Its lesson endures: the planet beneath our feet is ____.

For much of the twentieth century, cities in the United States required new buildings to provide a minimum number of off-street parking spaces: so many per apartment, per restaurant seat, or per square meter of office space. The rules were intended to keep drivers from crowding neighborhood streets. In his 2005 book The High Cost of Free Parking, the planning scholar Donald Shoup argued that these requirements carried enormous hidden costs. Parking spaces devour land and are expensive to build, especially in garages, and developers pass those costs on through higher rents and prices, even to residents who do not own cars. Mandatory parking also disperses buildings, making walking and public transit less practical and encouraging still more driving.
Persuaded by such critiques, a growing number of cities have abolished or reduced parking minimums. Buffalo, New York, became the first large American city to eliminate them citywide in 2017, and Minneapolis followed in 2021. In 2022 California barred most minimums near major public transit stops. Early studies suggest that developers still build parking where demand is strong but supply fewer spaces where it is weak, liberating land for housing and shops. The reform does not ban parking; it simply ____.

Nobody had warned me that a warehouse is loudest at five in the morning. Trucks reversed into the loading bays with shrill beeps, conveyor belts rattled overhead, and somewhere a radio played a song I could not quite make out. My supervisor, a compact woman named Delia, handed me a high-visibility vest and pointed to a forklift parked by the wall. I had passed the training course the week before, but the machine looked enormous now, and I was terrified of tipping a pallet of glass jars onto the concrete.
For the first hour I crept along the aisles so slowly that drivers behind me sighed and honked. Then Delia climbed onto the step beside me. She did not take the controls; she simply told me where to look, when to lower the forks, and when to trust the mirror rather than turning my head. By the end of the shift I had moved forty pallets without dropping a single jar. On my way out, Delia tossed me a packet of biscuits and said I would do. Coming from <u>her</u>, it felt like a medal.
